primary_summary: The video explains why the traditional prone Y‑raise limits lower‑trap activation because the thoracic spine extends when lying face‑down, compromising scapular congruence. It proposes a simple modification—placing the sternum over a ball to create a slight thoracic flexion—so the scapula can glide properly and the lower traps can work more effectively.

classification.usefulness_reason: Provides a clear biomechanical rationale and a concrete modification to improve lower‑trap activation in the prone Y‑raise.
problem_layers: poor scapular congruence in prone Y‑raise

problem_statements: Prone Y‑raise performed flat on the ground forces the thoracic spine into extension, which reduces scapular congruence and limits lower‑trap activation.
habits_or_contexts: performing prone Y‑raise without considering thoracic posture
key_visual_points: Spine naturally extends when lying face‑down
Scapula is a concave structure that needs to sit flush on a slightly convex thoracic cage
Placing the sternum over a small ball creates a gentle thoracic flexion
warnings_or_limitations: Avoid excessive slouching (over‑flexion) when using the ball

knowledge_units.title: Thoracic extension limits scapular glide during prone Y‑raise
knowledge_units.summary: When the thoracic spine is flat or extended in the prone position, the scapula cannot stay congruent with the rib cage, reducing the effectiveness of the lower traps.
observable_signs: Scapular winging or limited upward rotation
mechanisms: Thoracic extension pulls the scapula away from the rib cage
Reduced scapular glide impairs lower‑trap activation
errors_to_avoid: Lying completely flat on the floor
Allowing the thoracic spine to hyper‑extend
when_useful: When lower‑trap activation is poor during prone Y‑raise
when_not_useful: If the client already has adequate thoracic flexion

knowledge_units.title: Modified prone Y‑raise with sternum‑over‑ball placement
knowledge_units.summary: Place a small ball under the sternum while prone to induce a slight thoracic flexion, then perform the Y‑raise as usual.
observable_signs: Slight thoracic rounding maintained throughout the movement
mechanisms: Creates a gentle curvature in the thoracic spine, allowing the scapula to stay flush on the rib cage
execution_steps: 1. Position a small ball (e.g., yoga block) on the floor.
2. Lie prone and place the sternum directly over the ball.
3. Ensure the thoracic spine is gently rounded, not overly flexed.
4. Perform the Y‑raise, keeping the shoulders depressed and elbows slightly bent.
5. Maintain the ball contact throughout the set.
cues: Keep the thoracic spine mildly rounded
Feel the ball supporting the sternum
Avoid collapsing the chest into the floor
breathing_cues: Inhale to set up and create thoracic curvature
Exhale as you lift into the Y‑raise
errors_to_avoid: Removing the ball during the set
when_useful: Clients with limited thoracic extension during prone Y‑raise
when_not_useful: Clients with excessive thoracic kyphosis or pain in the upper back
